claim: The mouse neocortex is patterned into functionally distinct fields that include the primary sensory areas (visual, somatosensory and auditory), which receive modality-specific sensory inputs from thalamocortical axons (TCAs) originating from nuclei of the dorsal thalamus.
source: The mouse neocortex is patterned into functionally distinct fields that include the primary sensory areas (visual, somatosensory and auditory), which receive modality-specific sensory inputs from thalamocortical axons (TCAs) originating from nuclei of the dorsal thalamus (O'Leary et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to O'Leary et al., 2013

claim: In the cortex, the connections of TCAs establish precise topographic representations (or maps) of the sensory periphery.
source: In the cortex, the connections of TCAs establish precise topographic representations (or maps) of the sensory periphery (Krubitzer and Kaas, 2005; O'Leary et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Krubitzer and Kaas, 2005 and O'Leary et al., 2013

claim: Primary areas are flanked by higher order sensory areas (HO), which are interconnected with them and also contain topographic maps.
source: Primary areas are flanked by higher order sensory areas (HO), which are interconnected with them and also contain topographic maps (Felleman and Van Essen, 1991).
evidence: Supported by citation to Felleman and Van Essen, 1991

claim: In mammals, the evolutionarily conserved general layout of the intra-areal neural circuits is responsible for the orderly progression of sensory information, sensory perception and the integration of higher cortical functions.
source: In mammals, this evolutionarily conserved general layout of the intra-areal neural circuits is responsible for the orderly progression of sensory information, sensory perception and the integration of higher cortical functions (Felleman and Van Essen, 1991; Geschwind and Rakic, 2013; Krubitzer and Kaas, 2005; Laramée and Boire, 2014; O'Leary et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to Felleman and Van Essen, 1991; Geschwind and Rakic, 2013; Krubitzer and Kaas, 2005; Laramée and Boire, 2014; O'Leary et al., 2013

claim: Disrupted layouts of cortical area layouts appear to be associated with neurodevelopmental disorders including autism.
source: Disrupted layouts of cortical area layouts appear to be associated with neurodevelopmental disorders including autism (Courchesne et al., 2011; Voineagu et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Courchesne et al., 2011 and Voineagu et al., 2011

claim: Genetic mechanisms intrinsic to the neocortex control arealization during early cortical development.
source: Studies of cortical arealization, the mechanisms that pattern the neocortex into areas, have focused almost exclusively on the primary areas and have led to the prevailing model that genetic mechanisms intrinsic to the neocortex control arealization during early cortical development (Greig et al., 2013; Krubitzer and Kaas, 2005; O'Leary et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Greig et al., 2013; Krubitzer and Kaas, 2005; O'Leary et al., 2013

claim: The graded expression of the homeodomain transcription factor Emx2 in neocortical progenitors determines the size and position of the primary visual area (V1) in mice.
source: For example, the graded expression of the homeodomain transcription factor Emx2 in neocortical progenitors determines the size and position of the primary visual area (V1) in mice (Bishop et al., 2000; Hamasaki et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bishop et al., 2000 and Hamasaki et al., 2004

claim: Higher order areas outnumber primary areas by roughly 10-fold.
source: Although higher order areas outnumber primary areas by roughly 10-fold (Marshel et al., 2011; Wang and Burkhalter, 2007), mechanisms that specify them and define their proportions relative to primary areas have yet to be explored.
evidence: Supported by citations to Marshel et al., 2011 and Wang and Burkhalter, 2007

claim: Genetic manipulation of patterning genes, including Fgf17 and Emx2, results in altered V1 size.
source: Previous studies have shown that genetic manipulation of patterning genes, including Fgf17 and Emx2, results in altered V1 size (Cholfin and Rubenstein, 2007; Hamasaki et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citations to Cholfin and Rubenstein, 2007 and Hamasaki et al., 2004

claim: Transgenic mice that overexpress Emx2 (ne-Emx2) show area patterning defects including a V1 that is ~150% of the normal size, while retaining overall normal neocortex size.
source: Here we have analyzed transgenic mice that overexpress Emx2 (ne-Emx2) and show area patterning defects including a V1 that is ~150% of the normal size, while retaining overall normal neocortex size (Hamasaki et al., 2004 Leingärtner et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hamasaki et al., 2004 and Leingärtner et al., 2007

claim: The perimeters of primary sensory areas and the border between the neocortex and entorhinal cortex (ECT) can be visualized by serotonin (5HT) staining using a single postnatal day (P) 7 tangential section of the flattened cortical hemisphere.
source: By revealing the targeting patterns of TCAs projecting from thalamic sensory nuclei into the cortex (Fujimiya et al., 1986), the perimeters of primary sensory areas and the border between the neocortex and entorhinal cortex (ECT) can be visualized by serotonin (5HT) staining using a single postnatal day (P) 7 tangential section of the flattened cortical hemisphere (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by citation to Fujimiya et al., 1986 and reference to Figure 1A

claim: In ne-Emx2 brains, in addition to the previously reported enlarged V1, the cortical tissue that is nested between V1 and the surrounding primary areas and the ECT laterally appears qualitatively larger when compared to wildtype sections.
source: The staining shows that, in addition to the previously reported enlarged V1 (Hamasaki et al., 2004,; Leingärtner et al., 2007), the cortical tissue that is nested between V1 and the surrounding primary areas (primary somatosensory cortex: S1, auditory areas: Aud) and the ECT laterally appears qualitatively larger in ne-Emx2 brains, when compared to wildtype (wt) sections (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hamasaki et al., 2004 and Leingärtner et al., 2007, and by data shown in Figure 1A

claim: The caudal cortical territory outside of V1, S1, and the auditory areas showing no or weak 5HT staining contains the higher order visual areas surrounding V1, the retrosplenial cortex (RSC) medially, and the ventral posterior temporal cortex laterally.
source: We have defined this caudal cortical territory, which lies outside of V1, S1, and the auditory areas and shows no or weak 5HT staining as a joint higher order cortical area complex and have termed it HO-5HT. The 5HTstaining revealed that this region contains the higher order visual areas surrounding V1 (Wang and Burkhalter, 2007), the retrosplenial cortex (RSC) medially, and the ventral posterior temporal cortex laterally.
evidence: Supported by citation to Wang and Burkhalter, 2007

claim: Using P7 sagittal sections, the caudal 5HT-positive cortical area (corresponding to V1) and the anteriorly adjacent 5HT-negative area between V1 and S1 (corresponding to HO-5HT) appears larger in ne-Emx2 brains than in wt ones.
source: However, using P7 sagittal section, we confirmed in layer 4 that the caudal 5HT-positive cortical area (corresponding to V1) and the anteriorly adjacent 5HT-negative area between V1 and S1 (corresponding to HO-5HT) appears larger in ne-Emx2 brains than in wt ones (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1B

claim: Anterograde DiI labeling in the cortex revealed that TCAs from the dLG terminate in a smaller region in wt than in ne-Emx2 brains.
source: On the P7 sagittal sections that were derived from five different medial to lateral levels, anterograde DiI labeling in the cortex revealed that TCAs from the dLG terminate in a smaller region in wt than in ne-Emx2 brains (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1

claim: Across genotypes, the DiI staining revealed a sharp border with adjacent cortical tissues that did not receive TCAs input from the dLG.
source: Across genotypes, the DiI staining revealed a sharp border with adjacent cortical tissues that did not receive TCAs input from the dLG (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1

claim: The DiI staining indicates a well-defined border between V1 and neighboring higher order areas that is anteriorly shifted in ne-Emx2 brains.
source: This finding is consistent with the 5HT staining and indicates a well-defined border between V1 neighboring higher order areas that is anteriorly shifted in ne-Emx2 brains.
evidence: Inferred from DiI and 5HT staining data

claim: Cortical areas can be distinguished by area-specific gene expression patterns, which overlap with anatomical area borders and shift similarly when area patterning is disrupted.
source: Cortical areas can also be distinguished by area-specific gene expression patterns, which overlap with anatomical area borders and shift similarly when area patterning is disrupted (O'Leary et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to O'Leary et al., 2013

claim: Rorb expression is strongly induced by thalamic input to primary areas like S1 and V1 but is low in areas that do not receive their major inputs from the principal thalamic sensory nuclei, such as cortical higher order areas surrounding V1.
source: For example, Rorb expression is strongly induced by thalamic input to primary areas (Jabaudon et al., 2012) like S1 and V1 but is low in areas that do not receive their major inputs from the principal thalamic sensory nuclei, such as cortical higher order areas surrounding V1 (Chou et al., 2013; Wang and Burkhalter, 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to Jabaudon et al., 2012; Chou et al., 2013; and Wang and Burkhalter, 2007

claim: In ne-Emx2 brains, the high-to-low Rorb expression border is located more anteriorly, and the area showing low Rorb expression is larger than in wt sections.
source: In situ hybridization (ISH) on sagittal sections adjacent to 5HT-stained ones revealed sharp Rorb gene expression borders between areas in layer 4. Notably in ne-Emx2 brains, the high-to-low Rorb expression border is located more anteriorly, and the area showing low Rorb expression and resembling HO-5HT (Chou et al., 2013) is larger than in wt sections (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1B and citation to Chou et al., 2013

claim: Characteristic molecular markers that delineate the borders between V1 and surrounding higher order areas remain expressed at normal levels, but their sharp expression borders shift anteriorly in ne-Emx2.
source: This reveals that characteristic molecular markers that delineate the borders between V1 and surrounding higher order areas remain expressed at normal levels, but their sharp expression borders shift anteriorly in ne-Emx2.
evidence: Inferred from Rorb expression data

claim: Layer 5 corticotectal projections extended more anteriorly in ne-Emx2 sagittal sections.
source: We found that layer 5 corticotectal projections extended more anteriorly in ne-Emx2 sagittal sections.
evidence: Supported by data from DiI labeling experiments

claim: The layer 5 corticospinal projections extended less posteriorly in ne-Emx2 brains.
source: Vice versa, the layer 5 corticospinal projections extended less posteriorly in ne-Emx2 brains.
evidence: Supported by data from DiI labeling experiments

claim: The staining patterns of layer 5 projections are consistent with an altered balance of projection neuron identity in layer 5 and an overall expansion of visual areas.
source: These staining patterns are consistent with an altered balance of projection neuron identity in layer 5 (Greig et al., 2013; Zembrzycki et al., 2015) and an overall expansion of visual areas, demonstrating that areal patterning changes in ne-Emx2 brains are not limited to the cortical layers that receive thalamic input.
evidence: Inferred from layer 5 projection data and supported by citations to Greig et al., 2013 and Zembrzycki et al., 2015

claim: V1 and higher order area sizes are altered concomitantly in ne-Emx2 brains at the level of area-specific connectivity and gene expression in multiple cortical layers.
source: These findings complement previous reports describing Emx2 patterning functions (Bishop et al., 2000; Hamasaki et al., 2004; Leingärtner et al., 2003; Leingärtner et al., 2007) and indicate for the first time that V1 and higher order area sizes are altered concomitantly in ne-Emx2 brains at the level of area-specific connectivity and gene expression in multiple cortical layers.
evidence: Supported by data from multiple experiments and citations to Bishop et al., 2000; Hamasaki et al., 2004; Leingärtner et al., 2003; Leingärtner et al., 2007

claim: Changes in primary area size are paralleled by similar changes in higher order area size.
source: Taken together, our results suggest that changes in primary area size are paralleled by similar changes in higher order area size.
evidence: Inferred from the combined data on V1 and HO size changes

claim: Visual responses in V1 of wt and ne-Emx2 mice produced intrinsic signal maps that were indistinguishable in strength, and the axes of azimuth and elevation were organized in the same way in all tested brains.
source: Visual responses in V1 of wt and ne-Emx2 mice produced intrinsic signal maps that were indistinguishable in strength, and the axes of azimuth and elevation were organized in the same way in all tested brains (Figure 2A), revealing that functional topographic organization of the visual cortex was intact.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2A from Fourier intrinsic signal optical imaging

claim: The representations of elevation and azimuth were expanded in ne-Emx2 animals, and their retinotopic maps were overall larger (elevation: 138% ± 8.7% of wt; azimuth: 143% ± 8.2% of wt).
source: However, the representations of elevation and azimuth were expanded in ne-Emx2 animals, and their retinotopic maps were overall larger (elevation: 138% ± 8.7% of wt; azimuth: 143% ± 8.2% of wt).
evidence: Supported by quantitative data from intrinsic signal optical imaging

claim: The 5HT-stained V1 area accurately corresponds to the intrinsic functional V1 map.
source: On 5HT-stained, flattened tangential cortical sections, the DiI injection sites were found in all cases to be located near the border of the 5HT staining in V1, confirming the overall enlarged V1 perimeters in ne-Emx2 brains compared with the wt brains (Figure 2B). This shows that the 5HT-stained V1 area accurately corresponds to the intrinsic functional V1 map, suggesting that enlarged HO in ne-Emx2 brains have not acquired ectopic V1-like functional properties.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2B correlating DiI injection sites with 5HT staining

claim: Enlarged HO in ne-Emx2 brains have not acquired ectopic V1-like functional properties.
source: This shows that the 5HT-stained V1 area accurately corresponds to the intrinsic functional V1 map, suggesting that enlarged HO in ne-Emx2 brains have not acquired ectopic V1-like functional properties.
evidence: Inferred from the correspondence between 5HT staining and functional V1 map

claim: V1 is connected with the dLG, whereas the HO areas are wired to the posterior thalamic nucleus (PO).
source: Stereotypically, V1 is connected with the dLG, whereas the HO areas are wired to the posterior thalamic nucleus (PO) (Leyva-Díaz and López-Bendito, 2013; López-Bendito and Molnár, 2003).
evidence: Supported by citations to Leyva-Díaz and López-Bendito, 2013 and López-Bendito and Molnár, 2003

claim: In wt brains, when DiI was injected at the border between V1 and HO and DiD was injected into HO, retrogradely labeled green DiD cells were apparent in the dLG and the PO, while red DiI cells were only labeled in the dLG.
source: In representative cases (Figure 2C) where 5HT staining confirmed that DiI was injected at the border between V1 and HO and DiD was injected into HO, retrogradely labeled green DiD cells were apparent in the dLG and the PO. Conversely, red DiI cells were only labeled in the dLG.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2C from dual tracer experiments

claim: In ne-Emx2 brains, when DiI was injected into V1 and DiD was injected around the V1/HO border, red cells were found in the dLG, whereas green-labeled cells were apparent in the PO and the dLG.
source: In representative cases (Figure 2C) where 5HT staining confirmed that the DiI injection was administered into V1 and DiD was injected around the V1/HO border, red cells were found in the dLG, whereas green-labeled cells were apparent in the PO and the dLG.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2C from dual tracer experiments

claim: Although located more anteriorly in ne-Emx2 brains, the subcortical connectivity patterns around the V1/HO borders were similar to wt, demonstrating that these neurons show connectivity patterns that are consistent with their intrinsic areal identity and not their topographic location on the cortical sheet.
source: The dual tracings in wt and ne-Emx2 brains are consistent with the predicted connectivity of cortical neurons around the injection sites (Leyva-Díaz and López-Bendito, 2013; López-Bendito and Molnár, 2003). Although located more anteriorly in ne-Emx2 brains, the subcortical connectivity patterns around the V1/HO borders were similar, demonstrating that these neurons show connectivity patterns that are consistent with their intrinsic areal identity and not their topographic location on the cortical sheet.
evidence: Inferred from dual tracer data and supported by citations to Leyva-Díaz and López-Bendito, 2013 and López-Bendito and Molnár, 2003

claim: Increased V1 size in ne-Emx2 brains is accompanied by a concomitant enlargement and anterior shift of HO.
source: Taken together, our results indicate that increased V1 size in ne-Emx2 brains is accompanied by a concomitant enlargement and anterior shift of HO.
evidence: Inferred from combined data on V1 and HO size and position changes

claim: V1 gene expression domains of Unc5d and Igfbp5 were larger in ne-Emx2 brains (Unc5d-V1: 148% ± 6.1%, p = 0.0003; Igfbp5-V1: 148 ± 4.5%, p < 0.0001).
source: V1 gene expression domains of both markers were larger in ne-Emx2 brains (Unc5d-V1: 148% ± 6.1%, p = 0.0003; Igfbp5-V1: 148 ± 4.5%, p < 0.0001).
evidence: Supported by quantitative data from WMISH experiments

claim: The magnitude of the increased V1 size labeled genetically in ne-Emx2 brains is comparable to V1 area measurements derived from 5HT-stained P7 flattened cortical sections (5HT-V1: 142.1% ± 3.1%, p < 0.0001).
source: The magnitude of the increased in V1 size labeled genetically in ne-Emx2 brains is comparable to V1 area measurements derived from 5HT-stained P7 flattened cortical sections (Figure 3A: 5HT-V1: 142.1% ± 3.1%, p < 0.0001), indicating that molecular markers on whole brains reliably delineate V1 and can therefore be used to quantify and compare area sizes between samples and mouse lines.
evidence: Supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 3A

claim: Molecular markers on whole brains reliably delineate V1 and can be used to quantify and compare area sizes between samples and mouse lines.
source: The magnitude of the increased in V1 size labeled genetically in ne-Emx2 brains is comparable to V1 area measurements derived from 5HT-stained P7 flattened cortical sections (Figure 3A: 5HT-V1: 142.1% ± 3.1%, p < 0.0001), indicating that molecular markers on whole brains reliably delineate V1 and can therefore be used to quantify and compare area sizes between samples and mouse lines.
evidence: Inferred from comparison of genetic markers and 5HT staining data

claim: Cdh8 and Lmo4 expression is higher in the area surrounding V1, where higher order visual areas are located.
source: For example, Cdh8 and Lmo4 expression is higher in the area surrounding V1, where higher order visual areas are located (Chou et al., 2013; Marshel et al., 2011; Wang and Burkhalter, 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to Chou et al., 2013; Marshel et al., 2011; and Wang and Burkhalter, 2007

claim: The domains of high Cdh8 and Lmo4 expression appear to label higher order visual areas uniformly without revealing subdivisions between them.
source: The domains of high Cdh8 and Lmo4 expression appear to label higher order visual areas uniformly (Chou et al., 2013), without revealing subdivisions between them (compare schematic in Figure 3 showing approximate location and outline of higher order visual areas as identified by Wang and Burkhalter, 2007 to Cdh8 and Lmo4 gene expression domains around V1).
evidence: Supported by citation to Chou et al., 2013 and comparison to Wang and Burkhalter, 2007 data shown in Figure 3

claim: The size of the gene expression domains in V1 were similar in Cdh8- and Lmo4-stained brains (Cdh8-V1: 145.3 ± 7.4%, p < 0.0001; Lmo4-V1: 146.6% ± 6.7%, p = 0.0005).
source: The size (Cdh8-V1: 145.3 ± 7.4%, p < 0.0001; Lmo4-V1: 146.6% ± 6.7%, p = 0.0005) and shape of the gene expression domains in V1 were similar in Cdh8- and Lmo4-stained brains.
evidence: Supported by quantitative data from WMISH experiments

claim: The overall shapes of the two HO marker gene domains were similar and the sizes larger in ne-Emx2 brains compared with wt brains (Cdh8- HO: 145.7 ± 6.4%, p = 0.0015; Lmo4- HO: 144.9 ± 3.8%, p = 0.00157).
source: The overall shapes of the two HO marker gene domains were similar and the sizes larger in ne-Emx2 brains compared with wt brains (Cdh8- HO: 145.7 ± 6.4%, p = 0.0015; Lmo4- HO: 144.9 ± 3.8%, p = 0.00157).
evidence: Supported by quantitative data from WMISH experiments

claim: The analysis of different area-specific sets of marker genes revealed an increase in visually-related HO in ne-Emx2 brains that was proportionate to the V1 size increase.
source: The analysis of different area-specific sets of marker genes, either showing unique expression in V1, or discernable expression levels between visual areas, revealed an increase in visually-related HO in ne-Emx2 brains that was proportionate to the V1 size increase.
evidence: Inferred from quantitative data on V1 and HO marker gene expression

claim: The specific Lypd1 gene expression domain in the caudomedial cortex is significantly enlarged in ne-Emx2 brains (114.3 ± 5.2%, p = 0.0225, n = 4), compared with wt brains.
source: We found that the specific Lypd1 gene expression domain in the caudomedial cortex is significantly enlarged in ne-Emx2 brains (114.3 ± 5.2%, p = 0.0225, n = 4), compared with wt brains.
evidence: Supported by quantitative data from WMISH experiments

claim: The size increase of the RSC is not proportionate to the size increases of V1 and the higher order visual area complex labeled by Cdh8 and Lmo4 in ne-Emx2 brains.
source: This size increase is not proportionate to the size increases of V1 and the higher order visual area complex labeled by Cdh8 and Lmo4 in ne-Emx2 brains (Figure 3) suggesting that increased V1 size is specifically accompanied by a proportionate size increase of related higher order visual areas.
evidence: Inferred from comparison of RSC size increase to V1 and HO size increases shown in Figure 3

claim: Increased V1 size is specifically accompanied by a proportionate size increase of related higher order visual areas.
source: This size increase is not proportionate to the size increases of V1 and the higher order visual area complex labeled by Cdh8 and Lmo4 in ne-Emx2 brains (Figure 3) suggesting that increased V1 size is specifically accompanied by a proportionate size increase of related higher order visual areas.
evidence: Inferred from comparison of RSC, V1, and HO size changes

claim: Constitutive Emx2 mutant mice have an overall smaller brain and visual cortex, but homozygous mutants die perinatally.
source: Constitutive Emx2 mutant mice have an overall smaller brain and visual cortex, but homozygous mutants die perinatally (Bishop et al., 2000), preventing the analysis of cortical areas, which arise at later stages.
evidence: Supported by citation to Bishop et al., 2000

claim: Conditional, cortex-specific Emx2 mutant mice (cKO) are viable, fertile and have an anatomically normal neocortex.
source: These cKO mice are viable, fertile and have an anatomically normal neocortex (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2

claim: cKO brains show areal patterning changes that are similar to those previously reported in heterozygous Emx2 mutant brains but are opposite to those apparent in ne-Emx2 brains.
source: Confirming the prediction that reduced Emx2 expression levels in cortical progenitors would lead to smaller visual areas, cKO brains show areal patterning changes (Figure 4—figure supplement 3) that are similar to those previously reported in heterozygous Emx2 mutant brains (e.g. larger frontal cortex) (Hamasaki et al., 2004), but are opposite to those apparent in ne-Emx2 brains (e.g. smaller frontal cortex) (Hamasaki et al., 2004; Leingärtner et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3 and citations to Hamasaki et al., 2004 and Leingärtner et al., 2007

claim: V1 in cKO brains is greatly reduced in size.
source: As in ne-Emx2 brains, V1 in cKO brains was characterized using 5HT staining and DiI injections into the dLG (Figure 4—figure supplement 4), revealing that V1 in cKO is greatly reduced in size.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4

claim: Measurements of the molecular V1 marker domains revealed that the molecularly defined V1 in cKO was smaller than in wt brains (Unc5d-V1: 67.1 ± 2.6%, p = 0.00029; Igfbp5-V1: 68 ± 3.3%, p = 0.00017).
source: Measurements of the molecular V1 marker domains (Unc5d-V1: 67.1 ± 2.6%, p = 0.00029; Igfbp5-V1: 68 ± 3.3%, p = 0.00017), as well as the V1 expression domains of Cdh8 (67.7 ± 4.5%, p < 0.0001) and Lmo4 (68.6 ± 0.8%, p < 0.0001) revealed that the molecularly defined V1 in cKO was smaller than in wt brains.
evidence: Supported by quantitative data from WMISH experiments

claim: The V1 expression domains of Cdh8 and Lmo4 in cKO were smaller than in wt brains (Cdh8: 67.7 ± 4.5%, p < 0.0001; Lmo4: 68.6 ± 0.8%, p < 0.0001).
source: Measurements of the molecular V1 marker domains (Unc5d-V1: 67.1 ± 2.6%, p = 0.00029; Igfbp5-V1: 68 ± 3.3%, p = 0.00017), as well as the V1 expression domains of Cdh8 (67.7 ± 4.5%, p < 0.0001) and Lmo4 (68.6 ± 0.8%, p < 0.0001) revealed that the molecularly defined V1 in cKO was smaller than in wt brains.
evidence: Supported by quantitative data from WMISH experiments

claim: These reductions in V1 size matched the reduced V1 in 5HT-stained flattened cortex sections (5HT-V1: 68.5 ± 3%, p < 0.0001).
source: These reductions matched the reduced V1 in 5HT-stained flattened cortex sections (Figure 4A: 5HT-V1: 68.5 ± 3%, p < 0.0001).
evidence: Supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 4A

claim: Quantification of the gene expression domains of Cdh8 and Lmo4 surrounding V1 revealed that the cortical region that contains visually-related HO was also reduced in cKO brains to a degree proportional to the reduction in V1 size (Cdh8- HO: 66.8 ± 2.9%, p < 0.0001; Lmo4- HO: 69.3 ± 2.4%, p < 0.0001).
source: Subsequent quantification of the gene expression domains of Cdh8 and Lmo4 surrounding V1 (Figure 4B: Cdh8- HO: 66.8 ± 2.9%, p < 0.0001; Lmo4- HO: 69.3 ± 2.4%, p < 0.0001) revealed that the cortical region that contains visually-related HO was also reduced in cKO brains to a degree proportional to the reduction in V1 size.
evidence: Supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 4B

claim: When V1 size is reduced, related HO size is reduced to a similar extent.
source: These data demonstrate that when V1 size is reduced, related HO size is reduced to a similar extent.
evidence: Inferred from quantitative data on V1 and HO size reductions in cKO brains

claim: Ranging over an ~80% variation of the normal V1 size, related HO size is bi-directionally altered in a linear fashion (Cdh8 regression: y = −0.0071x + 1.7463; Lmo4 regression: y = 0.0208 + 1.7463).
source: Ranging over an ~80% variation of the normal V1 size, Figure 4C reveals that related HO size is bi-directionally altered in a linear fashion (Cdh8 regression: y = −0.0071x + 1.7463; Lmo4 regression: y = 0.0208 + 1.7463).
evidence: Supported by quantitative data and regression analysis shown in Figure 4C

claim: The size of V1 is determined by the activity of transcription factors including Emx2 during development, and this mechanism likewise controls the linear matching of the proportions of higher order visual areas in the mouse neocortex.
source: Taken together, our results are consistent with a proportional scaling relationship between the size of primary and related higher order visual areas: The size of V1 is determined by the activity of transcription factors including Emx2 during development, and this mechanism likewise controls the linear matching of the proportions of higher order visual areas in the mouse neocortex.
evidence: Inferred from combined data on V1 and HO size changes across genotypes

claim: Genetically altering the size of V1 over a range of ~80% of its normal size using a Emx2 gain-of function mouse line and a novel conditional Emx2 loss-of function mouse line showed that the specification of both primary and related higher order cortical areas during development was linearly scaled.
source: Genetically altering the size of V1 over a range of ~80% of its normal size using a Emx2 gain-of function mouse line and a novel conditional Emx2 loss-of function mouse line showed that the specification of both primary and related higher order cortical areas during development was linearly scaled by driving the unique properties that characterize both, V1 and higher order visual areas.
evidence: Supported by combined data from ne-Emx2 and cKO experiments

claim: Regardless of whether V1 was larger or smaller than in wt mice, related HO exhibited normal cytoarchitecture, genetic profiles, functional properties, and characteristic patterns of connectivity.
source: Regardless of whether V1 was larger or smaller than in wt mice, related HO exhibited normal cytoarchitecture, genetic profiles, functional properties, and characteristic patterns of connectivity that resulted in an overall uniformly altered 'visual cortical field' in the occipital cortex that remained accurately and proportionally subdivided into V1 and higher order visual areas.
evidence: Supported by combined data from multiple experiments on cytoarchitecture, gene expression, functional imaging, and connectivity

claim: Emx2 (and perhaps additional intrinsic area patterning regulators) specify a 'sensory cortical field' that includes primary and higher order areas and a defined border between them.
source: This demonstrates that Emx2 (and perhaps additional intrinsic area patterning regulators) specify a 'sensory cortical field' that includes primary and higher order areas and a defined border between them.
evidence: Inferred from combined data on V1 and HO specification and scaling

claim: This model of cortical area patterning is not consistent with the possibility that the core properties of primary and higher order areas are specified sequentially or through parallel genetic mechanisms.
source: This model of cortical area patterning is not consistent with the possibility that the core properties of primary and higher order areas are specified sequentially or through parallel genetic mechanisms.
evidence: Inferred from the linear scaling relationship between V1 and HO

claim: Higher order areas do not have a fixed size; rather their relative size is flexible.
source: Our results further reveal that higher order areas do not have a fixed size. Rather their relative size is flexible.
evidence: Inferred from data showing HO size changes proportional to V1 size changes

claim: Higher order areas scale linearly together with their related primary sensory areas.
source: By using mouse models with bi-directional changes of V1 size as a model, our study revealed that higher order areas scale linearly together with their related primary sensory areas,
evidence: Supported by quantitative data showing linear scaling relationship

claim: Cortical intrinsic mechanisms specify all generic primary and higher order visual cortex properties during early development.
source: In this model, cortical intrinsic mechanisms specify all generic primary and higher order visual cortex properties during early development.
evidence: Inferred from the observed genetic control of V1 and HO specification

claim: Geniculocortical input is needed to terminally differentiate the genetic distinctions between V1 and HO during postnatal development.
source: Much later during postnatal development, geniculocortical input is needed to terminally differentiate the genetic distinctions between V1 and HO (Chou et al., 2013; Vue et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Chou et al., 2013 and Vue et al., 2013

claim: Primary and related higher order areas remain proportionate when primary area size is altered through genetic mechanisms.
source: To the contrary, our results show that primary and related higher order areas remain proportionate when primary area size is altered through genetic mechanisms, suggesting that an increase in the complexity of connections and micro-circuits among higher order cortical processing centers likely accounts for gains in cortical functions that are characteristic for gyrencephalic mammals with larger cortical surface areas, compared to simpler lissencephalic mammals.
evidence: Supported by data showing linear scaling relationship

claim: An increase in the complexity of connections and micro-circuits among higher order cortical processing centers likely accounts for gains in cortical functions that are characteristic for gyrencephalic mammals with larger cortical surface areas, compared to simpler lissencephalic mammals.

claim: The newly discovered linear scaling relationship between primary and related higher order areas has major implications for the basic understanding of the development and organization of the neocortical bauplan and its evolution and variability in normal and affected conditions.

evidence: Speculative inference about broader implications of the findings
